The sound comes from a vibrating reed; the end of the chanter is closed, and traditional fingering lifts only one finger or opens one key at a time, so the range comes without overblowing and the tone is staccato and clear. The Northumbrian smallpipes are a bellows-blown bagpipe from northeast England, an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 422.111.2+422.22-62. The instrument usually has one keyed chanter and four drones; the chanter's bore is narrow and its end is closed, it is played by lifting a single finger or opening a single key, it takes its range without overblowing, and its sound is staccato and fairly quiet. It has long belonged to local musical culture, and its players include the official pipers of the Duke of Northumberland and the mayors of Gateshead and Newcastle, and it is also found in schools.
諾桑伯蘭小風笛用於英格蘭東北部的傳統音樂場合，常見於旋律加持續音的風笛演奏，也出: The Northumbrian smallpipes are played on traditional music occasions in northeast England, commonly in bagpipe playing that sets a melody over drones, and also in local dance tunes and variation sets. The repertoire includes reels, jigs, slip jigs and triple-time hornpipes, together with arrangements of Scottish, Irish and ballroom dance tunes. After the nineteenth century the keyed chanter made violin tunes easier to take over, such as "High Level" by James Hill. The Dukes of Northumberland, and the mayors of Gateshead and Newcastle, also keep a tradition of appointing official pipers.
